question.text: The newsvendor widget's expected value of perfect information (EVPI) comes out to 120 − 80 = 40. If a demand-forecasting service offered to sell a forecast for this problem, what should 40 be treated as?
options: An upper bound on what any forecast could be worth — a real forecast, being imperfect, is worth less than this
The exact fair price to pay for any forecast that improves on guessing
The minimum any useful forecast must be worth, since a worse forecast wouldn't be worth buying at all
The extra profit guaranteed once a forecasting service is under contract, regardless of its accuracy
question.hint: 'Perfect information' means knowing demand exactly, every time, before you decide. Does any real forecast do that?

explain.g: EVPI answers a specific, somewhat unrealistic question: what would it be worth to know the future exactly, every single time, before making a decision? Nobody sells that. It's useful precisely as a ceiling — a real forecast, which is right most of the time rather than always, can only be worth some fraction of this number, never more.
explain.y: EVPI = E[profit | perfect forecast] − E[profit at the stochastic optimum]. In this newsvendor instance (cost 2, price 5, demand 20 or 60 at probability ½ each), the stochastic-optimal order Q* = 60 earns 80 in expectation, while knowing demand in advance every time earns 120 — a 40 gap. That gap prices a forecast that is exactly right on every single occasion, which is the theoretical best case, not a service anyone can actually deliver.
explain.r: tools/verify_or5_or6.py runs both expected-profit calculations. In practice, the expected value of SAMPLE information — an imperfect but informative forecast — is what a real service would be priced against, and it is provably no greater than EVPI; 40 functions as a budget ceiling for evaluating whether a real forecast is worth its price, not a price itself.
